idiom_name: array of {function pointer, user data} + subscribe/unsubscribe/notify functions
implementation_notes: C has no subscription facility, so the roles are hand-written: a fixed or heap-allocated array of handler records (function pointer plus void* context) together with subscribe, unsubscribe and notify functions. The user-data pointer is what replaces the Observer object, and the function pointer replaces the Observer interface, which is why every realistic C observer API is built from this pair. Notify over a snapshot or a pending-removal flag, because a handler may unsubscribe while the loop runs.
pitfalls: The void* context is untyped: after the observer is freed it becomes a stale pointer that the next notification dereferences, so every subscribe needs a matching unsubscribe in the owner's teardown.
Iterating the live table while a handler unsubscribes skips handlers or reads freed memory; snapshot the array or mark entries for removal first.
A fixed-size handler array silently stops accepting subscribers once it is full unless subscribe reports the failure.

variants.name: GLib GObject signals (library)
variants.idiom_name: g_signal_connect / g_signal_emit / g_signal_handler_disconnect on a GObject type
variants.implementation_notes: Instead of writing the registry, a GObject-based program uses the library's signal system: signals are introduced per type and identified by name, user handlers are connected with g_signal_connect() and invoked in the order they were connected during a five-stage emission. GObject replaces the Observer interface with the GCallback placeholder plus a user_data pointer. Choose it when GLib/GTK is already in the stack; it is the C ecosystem's full realization of Observer, including per-instance handler lists and detail filtering.
pitfalls: Handlers are disconnected automatically only when the emitting object is finalised; if the user_data object dies first, the handler runs against freed memory - disconnect in its finalize, use g_signal_connect_data, or accept that g_signal_connect_object is unsafe in threaded programs.
Blocking a handler is counted, not idempotent: each g_signal_handler_block needs an equal number of unblocks before the handler runs again.
Emission stages (RUN_FIRST/RUN_LAST/RUN_CLEANUP, before/after handlers) make call order non-obvious, and a handler may stop the whole emission, silently skipping the rest.
